_about: Prepared defences (the grand campaign). An army that spends a whole month where it stands, without marching or fighting, digs in whoever commands it, the computer's armies as well as the player's. Against troops who are dug in and in supply the day's luck runs against the attacker, so that odds which would be safe in the open become a gamble, and an attack thrown back from such a line has shot its bolt for the month. Rules in src/campaign/game.ts (assess, resolveBattle, endPhase).

notes.entrench: 'auto': every corps in the field that ends its own month having neither moved nor fought is dug in from then on, unless it is under orders to give ground. Troops inside a town are not: its walls are their works. Trenches are lost the moment the corps leaves the ground. With 'auto' off only the player's corps under orders to dig do so, as in the historical scenarios. 'months': how long the works take to finish. A corps counts toward a prepared defence by the share of them it has had, so a line occupied last month is a third of the obstacle one held since the spring is.
notes.prepared: 'dice' is the run of the day's luck for an attack on defenders who are all dug in and in supply (in the open it is 0.8 to 1.2, and it takes 1.2 to 1 on the day to carry the ground). Where only part of the defence is prepared the run lies between the two in proportion, and massed guns in the attack take their share off it as they do off the trenches. 'spentAt': an attack that fails against a defence at least this far prepared leaves the attacking corps with no moves for the rest of the month. 'surprise': how much of its preparedness a line loses to the first two months of a new offensive by an army trained to it (Germany's). 'armour': how much it loses to an attack with tanks in it when the defence has no armour of its own. Both multiply with what the guns take off. 'losses': against a fully prepared line the attackers lose 'attacker' times the men they would in the open and the defenders 'defender' times, in proportion where the line is partly prepared.
notes.staff: 'odds': how much better odds than usual a computer staff asks before it attacks a fully prepared line. At 0 it attacks as it always did, and learns the cost in men.
notes.measured: Over 72 computer wars to the end of 1944 (Version 57 before, Version 58 after): Berlin fallen in 38 and 25, the German army still deep in Russia in 16 and 7, neither in 10 and 40; Paris falls between 2 and 3 months later. Of 36 wars run on to January 1947 Berlin had fallen in 29 and 7 were undecided. A dug-in, supplied line now throws back an attack at 1.5 to 1 about 4 times in 10 and at 2 to 1 about 1 in 7; nothing is safe under 2.4 to 1.
